author: Daron Acemoglu & Simon Johnson
title: Rebalancing AI (Power and Progress thesis essay)
central_scenario_summary: There is no inevitable path for AI: what matters for workers is marginal, not average, productivity, and the current 'just let AI happen' path—driven by the industry's AGI-focused paradigm—emphasizes automation (including 'so-so automation' with small gains) without the offsetting creation of new labor-complementary tasks, repeating the post-1970 imbalance that eroded shared prosperity. On this trajectory AI raises GDP only modestly, and its first-order impact is increased inequality within industrial countries, with middle- and lower-income countries also at risk. Five policy levers (business-model reform, symmetric taxation of labor and capital, labor voice, funding human-complementary research, government AI expertise) could redirect AI to complement worker expertise and restore shared prosperity.

quotes.text: AI could increase global GDP over the next five years, although not as substantially as enthusiasts claim. It might even modestly raise GDP growth in the medium term.

It is unclear how much this type of automation will contribute to aggregate productivity growth while these technologies are immature, but they could contribute to sizable productivity gains as costs fall and reliability improves.

capability_pace.notes: Explicitly skeptical of Goldman/explosive-growth forecasts; a real but gradual technology wave whose direction is a social choice.

quotes.text: While automation has maintained its pace or even accelerated over the ensuing five decades, the offsetting force of new task creation has slowed, particularly for workers without four-year college degrees.
AI offers an opportunity to complement worker skill and expertise if we direct its development accordingly.

expertise_erosion.notes: On the default path, non-college workers are pushed into low-paid services while gains accrue to those atop the skill/capital hierarchy—premia grow rather than erode. Their recommended path (AI for training/retraining educators, medical personnel, electricians, plumbers) would instead democratize expertise (would score 2); scored on the default trajectory. Judgment call.

productivity_breadth.notes: Modest aggregate gains on the current path, concentrated in automation of exposed tasks; larger gains possible later if reliability improves or development is redirected.

substitution.notes: Central/default trajectory is labor-displacing automation; complementarity is the counterfactual they advocate, not their prediction absent policy change.

quotes.text: Groceries do not become much cheaper, there is no expansion in food production, and shoppers do not live differently.
Even nontrivial productivity gains from automation can be offset when they are not accompanied by new tasks.

demand_absorption.notes: On the current path the productivity bandwagon fails: gains are too small and new task creation too weak for demand to generate offsetting jobs (contrast with their car-industry example where absorption worked). Mechanism is task creation rather than demand elasticities per se.

mobility_adjustment.notes: Displaced (especially non-college) workers reallocate only downward into low-paying services or face regional decline; no smooth adjustment expected on the default path.

rent_concentration.notes: Automation multiplies corporate profits without shared prosperity; power concentrates in a few tech firms/decision-makers absent competition policy and redirection.

timeline_years.notes: The essay's explicit forward horizon is the next five years to medium term; not a point estimate of a capability milestone.

inequality_prediction.score: On the current automation-focused trajectory, AI's first-order impact is increased inequality within industrial countries: automation raises average productivity and corporate profits without raising worker marginal productivity, and new task creation lags, especially for non-college workers. Middle- and lower-income countries also stand to lose, and there is no guarantee AI creates more jobs than it destroys—but redirecting AI toward human-complementary tasks could restore shared prosperity.

quotes.text: However, on our current trajectory, the first-order impact is likely to be increased inequality within industrial countries.
There is no guarantee that, on its current path, AI will generate more jobs than it destroys.
